chapter_theme: Opens the Swayamvara sarukkam: Tivittan after his victory, with the world at his feet, gives himself to pleasure; his chief queen asks to see the parijata tree wed to the Kamavalli creeper; and the brahmin jester Madhavan feigns a belly full of sweets, boasts of winning gifts in debate, and runs after fallen fruit in the grove.

cast.role: Tivittan, called the dark gem-hued lord, the king
the gods who guard the quarters
the sixteen thousand kings who bow
the sixteen thousand kings' daughters, his wives
the king's chief queen, named only by her rank
the queen's maid who carries the message
the brahmin jester, named Madhavan, the king's companion

1555.reading: The poet opens the new sarukkam, saying that after the dark-hued lord had destroyed the great ruler and was glad, he will tell of a further wealth that came to him.
1555.nuance: Tivittan is named only by his epithets here (மணிவண்ணன், the gem-hued one); the identification rests on the previous chapters. The first-person உரைக்கலுற்றேன் is the poet's own voice.
1555.event: The poet announces that another great fortune came to Tivittan after his victory.

1556.reading: After setting the world under a white umbrella like the full moon, the dark-lily-hued lord is caught in the net of deer-eyed women.
1556.nuance: The verse runs from rule to snare in one sentence: the umbrella that guards the world is followed at once by a net that holds the ruler.
1556.event: Having established his rule, Tivittan falls into the net of women's glances.

1557.reading: The dark-gem-hued lord takes on the sun's work, for the light of the gems in his crown drives off the thick darkness.
1557.event: Tivittan's crown-jewels light up the dark as the sun would.

1558.reading: Having gained the lotus, the conch and the other treasures and the seven jewels, the lord stands tall in body, eighty bows in height, and in his wealth.
1558.nuance: Only the lotus and the conch are named; the verse does not list the rest of the treasures, and the numbers (nine treasures, seven jewels) are the tradition's, not counted here.
1558.event: Tivittan gains the treasures and jewels of his wealth and stands eighty bows tall.

1559.reading: Sixteen thousand gods guard him from the quarters, sixteen thousand kings and a hundred and ten Vidyadhara kings bow, and the discus-bearer takes his pleasure like Kama.
1559.nuance: நூற்றொரு பதின்மர் is read as one hundred and ten. The verse sets the homage of all three realms beside a lover's ease and passes no judgement on either.
1559.event: Gods guard and kings and Vidyadhara kings bow to Tivittan while he takes his pleasure.

1560.reading: The sixteen thousand kings' daughters, like peahens, stand with the pollen of the flowers and a honey-rain pouring over their breasts as bees hum around them.
1560.nuance: Lines 3-4 are hard to construe (பில்கிய தேம்பெய் மாரி, துணருடை கின்ற); the reading holds the picture of women, pollen, honey and bees and no more.

1561.reading: One day the chief queen, seeing the parijata flower of the golden world put out buds, resolves to see the wedding of the tree and the young creeper called Kama.
1561.nuance: The verse treats a rite of marrying two plants as a courtly occasion; the tree is said to have come from a heavenly world (பொன்னணி உலகின்).
1561.event: The chief queen decides to see the parijata tree wed to the Kamavalli creeper.

1562.reading: The queen sends a bangled maid to tell the lord of the parijata's budding, and the maid bows to the king and makes the petition.
1562.event: The chief queen sends a maid to inform the king, and the maid petitions him.

1563.reading: The message says that the parijata, raised like a son by the women with water from their palms, is to be wed to the Kamavalli creeper, and the king is asked to understand the wish.
1563.nuance: The tree is spoken of as a son reared by the attendants, so the wedding is a family occasion; the next verse has the king repeat the word 'son'. The plural என்றார் may mean the queen's words are quoted by the maid.
1563.event: The maid delivers the queen's request that the reared parijata be wed to the creeper.

1564.reading: The king smiles and says that he will see the lady's son, at which the maid goes and the jester becomes the king's companion.
1564.nuance: 'The lady's son' is the parijata tree, so the king takes up the queen's way of speaking.
1564.event: The king agrees to see the plant 'son', and the jester takes his place at the king's side.

1565.reading: A man stands laughing with ear-rings, a golden curl and a garland knotted into his hair, one hand on his waist and the other holding his garment.
1565.nuance: He is not named until 1566 (அந்தணன்) and 1569 (மாதவன்); the identification follows 1564, which ends on the jester's arrival.
1565.event: The jester takes his place in comic dress and laughs.

1566.reading: Bent low before the king of spotless fame, the brahmin dances to the rhythm of a song.
1566.nuance: He is a brahmin, but a comic one; the poem gives him no Vedic learning in the verses that follow.
1566.event: The brahmin jester dances in front of the king to entertain him.

1567.reading: As the jester dances again and again with many beats, the long-crowned king laughs and calls it good.
1567.event: The king laughs and praises the jester's dance.

1568.reading: With his ear-rings slipping and his garment bunched about him, the jester puffs his belly out, rolls in the dust and groans.
1568.event: The jester puffs out his belly, rolls in the dust and groans.

1569.reading: Holding his belly, the man named Madhavan answers the king's question about his trouble by saying that it is full of many modakas, puffed up and swallowed.
1569.nuance: மாதவன் elsewhere means a great ascetic; for the jester it is either his name or an irony, and the reading cannot settle which.
1569.event: Asked what ails him, the jester says his belly is full of modakas.

1570.reading: Asked when he ate so many modakas, he says he has eaten none; they are to be eaten at the festival in the queen's fragrant grove.
1570.nuance: The joke turns on the time: his groaning is for a feast he has not yet eaten.
1570.event: The jester says the sweets are still to come, so that his belly is swollen with greed only.

1571.reading: The king laughs and asks what the trouble is, then says that no gift is given except to brahmins with Vedic tongues, and asks what he will do.
1571.nuance: The king states the rule as a tease to a glutton who has shown no learning; the work does not take it as its own teaching, and the jester answers with a joke, not an argument, so it is `reported`.
1571.event: The king tells the jester that gifts go only to Veda-learned brahmins.

claims.claim: gifts are due only to brahmins learned in the Veda

1572.reading: The jester says that he is skilled in debate, which can defeat the Veda-learned, and that he will get the gift that way; women have long known his merit.
1572.nuance: A boast of skill, not a doctrine: the jester sets debate-skill against Vedic learning as a title to the king's gift.
1572.event: The jester boasts that he can win the gift by beating the Vedic brahmins in debate.

1573.reading: He explains his way of winning debate: he will beat those who aim to win by recitation, with his stick, until his word prevails.
1573.nuance: The cudgel turns the idea of debate into a farce, so nothing of the debate's own arguments appears. The line 3 reading (தடியாலே) is not certain.
1573.event: The jester says his method of debate is to beat the reciters with a stick.

1574.reading: The king says 'good, let us see this debate', goes to the grove's wall gate with the guards, and enters the garden.
1574.event: The king goes with the guards to the grove gate and enters.

1575.reading: In the garden the jester in his mock dress runs about before the king and sees rich fruits fallen in heaps.
1575.event: The jester sees ripe fruit lying fallen in the grove.

1576.reading: At the sight of the fruit his mouth waters and his teeth run, and he runs to the king and says 'look, let us eat, let us eat'.
1576.event: The jester runs to the king and urges him to eat the fallen fruit.

1577.reading: A speaker, probably the king, says that if they are to pass this limit of the grove the other should come quickly, and then one of the two goes ahead singing loudly.
1577.nuance: Neither the speaker of lines 1-3 nor the one who walks ahead is named; the line 1 wording is obscure and the roles are inferred from 1574-1576.
1577.event: One of the pair urges the other to hurry on past the fruit and walks ahead singing.

1578.reading: The grove is full of sandal, mango and other trees whose bunched flowers bow down and shower honey and pollen like rain.

links.note: 1556 shows the king settled under the moon-white umbrella; Naladiyar 3 says kings who rode under umbrellas have fallen when their deeds turned.
links.teaches: The poem sets Tivittan at the top of his glory, and the quatrain supplies the warning that such a place is held by deeds and can be lost.

gains.a: The opening praise gains a measure that the umbrella is no guarantee, so the lord's net of women reads as a risk.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a king shown at his height with no fall yet in sight, which is the moment it speaks to.

links.note: 1559 shows a king with the homage of three realms taking pleasure like Kama; Naladiyar 60 says the higher ones see the pain in pleasure and do not cling.
links.teaches: The poem offers pleasure at its largest scale, and the quatrain asks whether one who has all of it is looking at its pain.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which a lord in his harem is judged without the poet having to judge him.
gains.b: The quatrain gains an extreme case of the pleasure it warns about, with gods and kings standing guard over it.

links.note: 1561 has the chief queen resolve to see the plants wed; in 1564 the king smiles and accepts, and the grove outing follows.
links.teaches: The queen's wish becomes the king's plan only through the maid's message and his answer, so the outing is shared.

links.note: 1569 has the jester say his belly is full of many modakas; 1570 has him deny eating any.
links.teaches: His pain is only greed for a feast to come, so the first claim is turned into a joke by the second.

links.note: 1571 limits the king's gifts to Vedic brahmins; 1572 has the jester answer that debate-skill will win them.
links.teaches: The rule meant to bar the jester is met by a claim that skill in debate can stand in for Vedic learning.

links.note: 1571 has the king test a gift-seeker by Vedic learning; Kural 134 says a Brahmin can relearn the Veda but loses his birth if conduct fails.
links.teaches: The king's test is of learning, and the couplet's is of conduct, so the jester's comic case falls under both and passes neither.

gains.a: The king's rule gains a rival test, so the gift is shown to rest on a narrow ground.
gains.b: The couplet gains a brahmin who has neither Veda nor conduct and appears at the king's court.

links.note: 1572 has the jester boast of winning debates; 1573 gives his method, a stick for those who recite.
links.teaches: The boast gets its method, which shows that his debate is a comic beating, not an argument.

links.note: 1573 has the jester win debate by beating reciters; Tirumanthiram 51 says the wise gave up disputation and recited the Veda to gain release.
links.teaches: The jester practises debate for a gift and the verse in the Tirumanthiram says the wise leave debate for recitation, so the farce is set against that view.

gains.a: The jester's boast gains a standard against which debating for a gift looks like a caricature of the learned.
gains.b: The Tirumanthiram's rejection of disputation gains a figure for whom argument has become a way to get food.

links.note: 1576 has the jester at the fallen fruit with his mouth watering; 1569 has him holding a belly full of modakas.
links.teaches: The same belly-led jester returns, now drooling instead of groaning, so greed is drawn as his trait and not one joke.

source_issues: Verses 1555-1558, 1562-1565 and 1569 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1560 lines 3-4 and 1577 line 1 are hard to construe; the readings are marked uncertain.
1563 has the plural என்றார் where 1564 implies the maid (என்றவள்) spoke.
